references.text: Jesus' parallel statement in Matthew: 'Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.' This is the direct parallel to Luke 11:23.
Jesus says: 'Whoever is not against us is for us.' This appears to be a complementary statement that illuminates the same truth from another angle—there is no neutral ground in relation to Jesus.
Luke's own parallel to Mark 9:40, where Jesus says: 'Whoever is not against you is for you.' Together with Luke 11:23, this shows that neutrality toward Jesus is impossible.
The context of Jesus' words in Matthew: the debate over Beelzebul and the casting out of demons. The same context as Luke 11:23—Jesus defends that he casts out evil spirits by the finger of God.
The immediate context in Luke: Jesus' defense against the accusation that he casts out demons by Beelzebul. Verse 23 is the conclusion of this argument—one is either with Jesus or against him.
Joshua meets the commander of the Lord's army, who demands absolute loyalty. The question 'Are you for us or for our enemies?' illustrates the same principle: before God there is no neutrality.

Elijah challenges the people on Mount Carmel: 'How long will you waver between two opinions?' The demand to choose a side between the Lord and Baal reflects Jesus' requirement in Luke 11:23 that one cannot be neutral.

The message to the church in Laodicea: because they are lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, the Lord will spit them out. This underscores the same principle as Luke 11:23—a half-hearted attitude toward Christ is unacceptable.
